https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/summer-mu.text: Melanie McDonagh Sun, 19 July 2026 at 5:47 am UTC 0 A blistering summer is hardly the time when you want to be in the kitchen, but it is, very much, when you want to eat something light and delicious. You can’t go wrong, obviously, with Elizabeth David’s Summer Cooking (£10.89, Amazon.co.uk ), but there are several new and inviting possibilities out there to try. 'Sunshine, Lemons and Sea Salt' by Donna Hay, published by Fourth Estate Absolute summer food porn, this is liberally illustrated with pictures of Donna Hay’s own seaside home, full of roses and covetable vintage tableware. Hay is Australia’s answer to Delia Smith, with a free and easy approach to cooking and a bent for flavoursome, easy-on-the-eye dishes. Nothing’s difficult and she talks you through recipes like a friend. I like her unscrupulous short cuts; her cheat’s ice creams combine shop-bought ice cream with frozen fruit. Yum. For £200, real groupies can buy a Donna Hay hamper from Fortnum & Mason with her favourite ingredients, plus the book. Buy now £23.00, Amazon.co.uk 'The Kitchen Book' by Ella Risbridger, published by Fourth Estate If the success of a cookbook can be measured by the filthiness of the pages then this, from Ella Risbridger, is already a winner. There is no one who writes more invitingly about food, cajoling you into trying this delicious assembly or that. And her recipes are indeed easy and delicious. But it’s the inviting prefaces that draw you in; her little essay persuading you that a bowl of radishes in ice cold water with butter is all you really want to eat is billed as Radishes for Company. Also, how can you not like a girl who suggests you serve roast potatoes at a party? Buy now £21.00, Amazon.co.uk 'La Trattoria' by Dara Klein, published by Ebury Dara Klein’s restaurant, Tiella on Columbia Road, is already a hit and here is the book of the restaurant and her family’s culinary adventures. Subtitled Intuitive Italian cooking, this is a reassuringly classic account of the whole tradition of the trattoria, from bar snacks to desserts. There are lots of old favourites, including ribollita (bread and vegetable soup), caponata (aubergine and tomato) and zabaglione (boozy custard). But you know what? These staples are popular for a reason — they’re what you want to eat. Buy now £23.00, Amazon.co.uk 'The Italian Table' by Theo Randall, published by Quadrille Another homage to Italy comes from Theo Randall, who offers 100 irresistible recipes with the most inviting photography. Many are very simple — asparagus with fried eggs and parmesan, say — and the pasta dishes are terrifically inviting, though the filled ones need a pasta machine. Excellent desserts, too. Randall has a natural affinity with the simplicity of the best Italian cooking and a feel for the regional character of dishes. His recipe for porchetta is delicious. Buy now £17.24, Amazon.co.uk 'The Coastal Forager' by Mark Williams, published by Skittledog Let me fess up; I haven’t actually tried out this excellent book — subtitled Wild Maritime Food to Preserve, Cook and Eat — yet, because I won’t be anywhere near the sea until August. But I’ve been wanting for ages to be able to identify and cook with seaweed, and this is a really helpful guide to identifying the umpteen varieties, harvesting them and cooking with them. It’s not just seaweed, though is there anything more fashionable than dulse? There are sections on the plants and fruits that flourish near the sea, including Alexanders and sea buckthorn. The lovely painted illustrations by Sofia Iva and photographs make identification easy. This is in fact a guide to responsible foraging. There’s also a section on shellfish… apparently limpets are tasty. When I next go to the beach it will be with purpose, a bucket and a copy of The Coastal Forager. Buy now £28.00, Blackwells.co.uk 'Viennese Bakery' by Bernadette Worndl, published by DK Oh boy, I’ve been waiting a long time for this, a really good collection of recipes for Viennese cakes and pastry, the kind you’d get in the best cafés. There is nothing more heavenly than cakes like these. Bernadette Worndl’s Viennese Bakery has the lot: Sachertorte, strudels, yeasted plum cake, Esterhazy cake. Some are complex, lots are easy and many evoke Austria’s imperial past and its grand culinary traditions. The Empress Elisabeth never told the Austria-Hungarians to go and eat cake because they didn’t need telling. Buy now £18.85, Amazon.co.uk 'Lateral Cooking' by Niki Segnit, published by Bloomsbury This is a sequel to Niki Segnit’s fabulous Flavour Thesaurus and is based on “a series of starting points which, once you’re familiar with them, will prove almost infinitely adaptable”. So, a simple bread dough gets you quickly to pizza and croissants and umpteen variants. A batter mix gives you pancakes, then Yorkshire puddings and so on to churros. Each basic recipe is followed by a series of suggestions for taking it further. It all makes resounding sense. This is not just a genius cookbook, it’s also a hoot to read… our author is authoritative and funny. The cookbook of the year. Rețele Electrice România surpasses 2 million smart meters, on track for 67% coverage by end of 2026 Energy News Top stories Published on August 26, 2026 By Petre Barac Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Rețele Electrice România, the electricity distribution operator for Muntenia Sud, Banat and Dobrogea, has installed more than 2 million smart meters. Launched in 2015 under a plan approved by ANRE, the rollout continues in 2026 with about 178,000 additional new-generation meters that communicate through a hybrid system combining PLC and radio-frequency (RF) technology and is set to bring coverage to 67% by year-end (2.164 million meters out of about 3.2 million consumption points across the three regions). Mihai Stancu, Head of Customer Engagement at Rețele Electrice România, spoke with The Diplomat-Bucharest about what this means in practice for consumers: how their data stays protected, and how artificial intelligence is already starting to play a role in customer service. What is a smart meter and how does it differ from a classic meter? A smart meter is a measuring device from a modern generation that automatically and securely transmits energy consumption to the distributor without the need to manually read the index. Unlike a classic meter, it records consumption on hourly intervals, allows billing on real consumption and shortens the time to solve technical and commercial operations, many of which can be carried out remotely, without a home visit. Data communication is done securely, through PLC (power-line communication) technology, and the new generation of meters, introduced from 2026, uses a hybrid system, which combines PLC with radio-frequency (RF) transmission, for more stable communication. Integrated into an intelligent metering system, the meter communicates directly with us, the distributor and the customer, who can track their consumption in the online account. How many smart meters has Reţele Electrice România installed and what is the target for the coming years? Reţele Electrice România has already exceeded the threshold of 2 million smart meters installed, the largest volume implemented by a distribution operator in Romania. In 2026, the company will install approximately 178,000 new generation meters, so that the goal for the end of this year is a coverage of 67%, with a total of 2.164 million meters, out of the approximately 3.2 million consumption places in Muntenia Sud, Banat and Dobrogea. The program, started in 2015, continues according to the plan approved by ANRE. What are the concrete benefits of the smart meter for the consumer? The smart meter brings the customer several direct benefits. The first is billing on the actual consumption measured, instead of an estimate, because the index is transmitted automatically and without errors. The second is the monitoring of their own consumption by days and time intervals, directly from the online account, which helps the customer to understand their consumption behavior and reduce the bill. The meter allows the use of several tariff types and opens access to differentiated offers on time slots. Moreover, it provides the consumption data necessary for contracts with dynamic prices, correlated with the evolution of the energy market, with hourly or even 15-minute recording. Thus, the customer can benefit from lower prices in the intervals when energy is cheap and can move his consumption to those periods. For customers who become prosumers, the smart meter is already ready: it measures both the energy consumed from the grid and the energy produced and delivered to the grid, without the need for a new meter replacement when installing the photovoltaic panels. This simplifies and speeds up the connection process as a prosumer. In addition, switching providers, connections and disconnections can be done remotely, and reconnecting after an incident is faster. The replacement of the old meter with a smart one is done at no additional cost to the customer, according to ANRE regulations. How does the digitalization of the grid help reduce power outages? The digitalization of the network shortens the time a customer is left without power. Through the remote control points, of which we have installed 575 in 2025 alone, we monitor and control the network remotely, in real time. When a defect occurs, we can locate and isolate it in a few minutes, instead of a few hours, and some interventions are done remotely. The effect can be seen in the quality indicators: the average duration of unplanned outages per customer (SAIDI) reached an average of 79.39 minutes in 2025 for the three regions of the Rețele Electrice România (Muntenia Sud, Banat and Dobrogea), compared to about 700-800 minutes in 2005. How are customer consumption data collected through smart meters protected? Consumption data is transmitted securely, through PLC technology on the electrical wire, and to the new generation of meters through a hybrid system, which combines PLC with radio-frequency (RF). The meter communicates via a data concentrator to the distributor’s central system, in accordance with European and national data protection rules. Consumption data is only accessible to the consumer and his supplier. Any sharing to another supplier is made exclusively at the consumer’s initiative, from his or her online account, through the “Delegation of POD Potential Supplier” service, which gives temporary access to the consumption history, for 7 calendar days. How does artificial intelligence and smart meter data help better customer and supplier service? Artificial intelligence and data from smart meters help us provide better service to both customers and suppliers. At the end of 2024, we put into operation an IT platform through which all energy suppliers receive daily consumption data from customers with smart meters from the 11 counties in our area, together with load curves, for more accurate forecasts and more suitable offers. In 2025, the average monthly number of remote readings was around 2 million, which means fewer trips and a smaller carbon footprint. For customers, we are already using artificial intelligence in the connection process, in document analysis and in estimating the average connection time, and the direction we are going is to integrate artificial intelligence into the information flow, so that each customer receives real-time details about their request. What does a prosumer need to do to connect to the grid and how does smart metering help? A prosumer is a customer who produces energy, usually with photovoltaic panels, and can deliver it to the grid. For the connection, he can submit the application and the necessary documents online to Rețele Electrice România, receive the technical approval for the connection, depending on the requested power, and, after installing the installation, the prosumer certificate. This is where the smart meter plays an essential role: with the bidirectional measurement function, it records the energy delivered to the grid and the energy absorbed from the grid separately. Thus, the prosumer knows exactly when he consumes from the grid and when he uses the renewable energy that he produces himself. Photograph: Ibrahim Ndamitso/Reuters Nigeria Survivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 died Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children Eromo Egbejule in Abidjan and agencies Fri 18 Sep 2026 13.27 EDT First published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 11.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Survivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna. The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal gold mines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger. NSCDC – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths on a disease outbreak. However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible. The state governor, Umar Bago, said many of the dead were children, aged 14 to 18, who had been working in the mines instead of going to school. “There are issues of illegal mining and it is taking a toll on our children,” he said. Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.” A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background. AFP reported that another survivor, who asked not to be named, said he had made it out alive because he was near the cell’s entrance, where he could breathe better. “We were screaming for help,” he said, with detainees telling the guards that “people are dying one after the other. They did not believe us.” President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ordered an investigation into the deaths after his government earlier suspended some senior officials. But protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas. A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – ​some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called ‌for justice. Some protesters tried ‌to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make ‌a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order. View image in fullscreen Family members outside Minna general hospital. Protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in the city. Photograph: Ibrahim Ndamitso/Reuters As ⁠curfew began at 6pm local time on Friday, security forces appeared to have at least temporarily restored order to the streets of the city. The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of an investigation. Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and is more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to The Long Wave Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world after newsletter promotion Police and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died. “It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations. The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits. Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report. Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.
